name: New Netherland
info: The Dutch Republic's fur-trading colony on the Hudson and Delaware, run by the West India Company from New Amsterdam on Manhattan until England took it in 1664 and kept it by the Treaty of Breda.

facts.capital: New Amsterdam, on Manhattan (Fort Amsterdam, from 1626; the seat had first been meant for the South River)
facts.founder: The New Netherland Company's traders under the States General's patent of 1614; the Dutch West India Company (chartered 1621), whose first director was Cornelius Jacobsen May
facts.predecessor: The lands of the Lenape, Mahicans and Mohawks, visited by Henry Hudson for the Dutch East India Company in 1609
facts.successor: The English Province of New York, after the surrender of New Amsterdam to Richard Nicolls on 27 August 1664, confirmed by the Treaty of Breda (1667)

t: The colony existed for the fur trade: the Dutch depended on Native nations to capture, skin and deliver beaver pelts, and after the Mohawks conquered the Mahicans in 1628 they held a near-monopoly of that trade.
Peter Minuit acquired Manhattan from unnamed Native people on 24 May 1626 for goods worth 60 guilders, a figure a historian turned into the famous $24 in 1846 by a faulty conversion.

Its 1664 Articles of Capitulation kept the liberty of conscience New Netherlanders already enjoyed, and the Flushing Remonstrance of 1657 is counted a precursor of the religious-freedom clause in the United States Bill of Rights.
dyk: New Amsterdam's wal, the rampart that gave Wall Street its name, was built out of fear of an English invasion; when four English frigates finally came in 1664 the town surrendered without resistance.
ev: Henry Hudson, hired by the Dutch East India Company, sails the Halve Maen into Upper New York Bay and up the river that bears his name as far as the site of Troy.
On 17 March the States General grants an exclusive trade patent between the 40th and 45th parallels; traders of the New Netherland Company build Fort Nassau near Albany.
On 3 June the Dutch Republic charters the Dutch West India Company with exclusive rights in West Africa and the Americas.
New Netherland becomes a province; 30 families land at Fort Orange and Noten Eylant from the ship Nieu Nederlandt under Cornelius Jacobsen May, the first director.
On 24 May Peter Minuit and Walloon colonists acquire Manhattan for goods worth 60 guilders and build Fort Amsterdam at its southern tip.
The Charter of Freedoms and Exemptions creates the patroonships; Rensselaerswyck becomes the only truly successful one.
Director-general Peter Stuyvesant conquers New Sweden on the Delaware; Jews are granted full residency in New Amsterdam.
On 27 August four English frigates under Richard Nicolls demand the surrender of New Amsterdam, which falls without resistance.

sections.foundation:
In 1609 the English captain Henry Hudson, hired by the Dutch East India Company to find a passage to Asia, sailed the flyboat Halve Maen into Upper New York Bay and up the river now named for him until the water grew too shallow at the site of Troy. He reported fertile land and people willing to barter furs. Between 1611 and 1614 Adriaen Block, Hendrick Christiaensen and Cornelius Jacobsen May charted the coast from Maryland to Massachusetts, and Block's map was the first to carry the name New Netherland. Juan Rodriguez, born in Santo Domingo of Portuguese and African descent, wintered on Manhattan in 1613–1614 trading for the Dutch, the first recorded non-Native inhabitant of the future New York City.

On 17 March 1614 the States General offered an exclusive patent for trade between the 40th and 45th parallels, won by the New Netherland Company, whose traders built Fort Nassau on Castle Island near Albany; flooding forced its abandonment when the patent expired in 1618. On 3 June 1621 the Republic chartered the Dutch West India Company with exclusive rights in West Africa and the Americas. In 1624 New Netherland became a province, and in May the company landed 30 families at Fort Orange and Noten Eylant from the Nieu Nederlandt under May, its first director; 45 more colonists and 103 animals followed in 1625. Many settlers were Walloons, French Huguenots or Africans, most of the last enslaved.
sections.socioeconomy:
Like the French to the north, the Dutch came for furs. Their first partners were the Algonquins, and they depended on Native nations to capture, skin and deliver pelts, above all beaver; after the Mohawks of the Iroquois Confederacy conquered the Mahicans in 1628, they held a near-monopoly of the trade through the Adirondacks and the Mohawk Valley. New Amsterdam, outside Fort Amsterdam, became a hub for trade between North America, the Caribbean and Europe, loading pelts, lumber and tobacco. The Charter of Freedoms and Exemptions of 1629 granted vast patroonships with manorial courts and the duty to settle 50 tenants in four years; of the five, only Rensselaerswyck, at the head of navigation on the North River, truly succeeded.

The colony's people were never only Dutch. Not counting Native Americans, the population was 4,301 in 1650 and 8,000 to 9,000 at the transfer of 1674; Dutch was the official language beside French, Scandinavian and German tongues and Algonquian languages. The company introduced slavery in 1625 with eleven enslaved Africans who worked as farmers, fur traders and builders. They were admitted to the Reformed Church, could testify in court, sign documents and sue whites, some earned wages equal to white workers', and families were usually kept together; some later gained "half-free" status, and when the colony fell the company freed its slaves, forming an early nucleus of free Black people.
sections.military:
New Netherland was a chain of garrisoned trading stations rather than an armed state. Company policy required land to be bought from the Indians, but the Dutch took their gifts of sewant and goods as exclusive title while the Lenape bands meant to share, not leave, and the misunderstanding bred violence. Director Willem Kieft (1638–1647) demanded tribute from the Tappan and Wecquaesgeek, who ignored him, then, against the advice of his own Council of Twelve Men, ordered attacks at Pavonia and Corlear's Hook on groups who had taken refuge with the Dutch from their Mohican enemies. The massacre left 130 dead; the surrounding tribes united and raided the province for two years, until a treaty brokered largely by the Hackensack sagamore Oratam ended Kieft's War in 1645.

On the Delaware the patroons' settlement of Zwaanendael was destroyed by the local Indigenous population soon after its founding in 1631, and in 1638 Peter Minuit, now in Swedish service, planted New Sweden at Fort Christina; New Amsterdam could only protest. The Dutch built Fort Casimir in 1651, lost it to the Swedes in 1654, and in 1655 Stuyvesant led the expedition that conquered New Sweden, renaming its chief settlement New Amstel. Against England the colony had no defence: appeals for troops were ignored, and when Richard Nicolls's four frigates arrived on 27 August 1664 New Amsterdam surrendered without a shot.
sections.governance:
New Netherland was a company colony. The Dutch West India Company appointed its directors, Cornelius Jacobsen May in 1624, Willem Verhulst in 1625, Peter Minuit from 1626, Willem Kieft from 1638 and Peter Stuyvesant from 1647, the only one styled director-general. Director and council together held executive and legislative power and sat as the court of justice. The colonists, vocal and quick to challenge authority, submitted the Remonstrance of New Netherland, written by the Leiden-educated lawyer Adriaen van der Donck, condemning the company's mismanagement and demanding full rights as citizens of the Netherlands; after three years' wrangling the Dutch government granted a measure of self-government and recalled Stuyvesant in April 1652, orders rescinded a month later when the First Anglo-Dutch War broke out. New Amsterdam got its municipal charter in 1653.

The company made the Reformed Church the official institution, but the Union of Utrecht's rule that no one be persecuted for religion was written into the first instructions of 1624: colonists were to win Indians and non-believers "through attitude and by example" and leave everyone the freedom of his conscience. The rule prevailed twice against Stuyvesant's narrow outlook, in the grant of full residency to Ashkenazi and Sephardi Jews in New Amsterdam in 1655 and in the Flushing Remonstrance of 1657, when some thirty residents petitioned against his ban on Quaker worship.
sections.impact:
The colony's reach was commercial and lasting. Its trade tied the Iroquois and Algonquian fur country to Amsterdam and the Caribbean, and its claims shaped the map: by the Treaty of Hartford of 1650 Stuyvesant provisionally ceded the Connecticut River region to New England, setting the eastern border 50 Dutch miles west of the river's mouth and just west of Oyster Bay on Long Island, a line the company refused to recognise but which held in practice. New Netherland grew into what is now the largest metropolitan area in the United States, and writers have argued that its "secular broadmindedness and mercantile pragmatism" and its financial rather than religious motive set New York on a different course from the other colonies; William Byrd remarked in 1682 that it had as many sects as Amsterdam.

Its legal legacy ran through the Articles of Capitulation of 1664, whose Article VIII kept the liberty of conscience and which were incorporated into later city, state and national constitutions, and through the Flushing Remonstrance, counted a precursor of the Bill of Rights' provision on religious freedom. The Roosevelts descend from Claes van Roosevelt, who came about 1650; Martin Van Buren grew up in Kinderhook speaking only Dutch. The flags of New York City, Albany and Jersey City carry the colours of the Prinsenvlag, the feast of Saint Nicholas gave Santa Claus, and Dutch names such as Manhattan, Catskill and Red Hook remain.
sections.decline:
The colony was always outgrown. English settlers from Massachusetts Bay moved onto the Fresh River and Long Island from 1637, with or without Dutch leave, and the New England Confederation of 1643 took in Connecticut and New Haven on land the United Provinces claimed; the Dutch could neither people nor defend their claim. In March 1664 Charles II resolved to annex New Netherland and bring all his kingdoms under one government in church and state. The company's directors hoped the religious freedom they offered would keep the English settlers loyal, but when Nicolls's frigates came on 27 August 1664 the defenceless town yielded, Stuyvesant negotiating good terms from his "too powerful enemies". On the Delaware Colonel Sir Robert Carr broke them, seizing property and selling Dutch prisoners of war into slavery, and Pieter Corneliszoon Plockhoy's Mennonite settlement near Lewes was destroyed.

The Treaty of Breda of 1667 ended the Second Anglo-Dutch War; the Dutch did not press their claim, keeping Suriname and the nutmeg island of Run instead. In August 1673 Evertsen and Binckes retook the colony, Anthony Colve governed it and the city was renamed New Orange, but the Republic, exhausted by the disaster years of 1672–1674, gave it up by the Treaty of Westminster in February 1674; on 10 November 1674 Edmund Andros took over from Colve. Dutch speech, law and 8,000 to 9,000 New Netherlanders passed into the Province of New York.

summary: New Netherland, the Dutch West India Company's colony on the Hudson and Delaware from the patent of 1614, lived by the beaver trade with the Mohawks and Lenape, grew fast in the 1650s around New Amsterdam, and fell without a fight to English frigates in 1664; the Treaty of Breda of 1667 left it to England, with its liberty of conscience intact.
references: Jaap Jacobs, The Colony of New Netherland: A Dutch Settlement in Seventeenth-Century America (Cornell University Press, 2009)
Oliver A. Rink, Holland on the Hudson: An Economic and Social History of Dutch New York (Cornell University Press, 1986)
Russell Shorto, The Island at the Center of the World: The Epic Story of Dutch Manhattan and the Forgotten Colony That Shaped America (Doubleday, 2004)
Donna Merwick, The Shame and the Sorrow: Dutch-Amerindian Encounters in New Netherland (2006)
Edwin G. Burrows and Mike Wallace, Gotham: A History of New York City to 1898 (1999)
Janny Venema, Beverwijck: A Dutch Village on the American Frontier, 1652–1664 (State University of New York Press, 2003)

pointDescs.1614: The States General grants the trade patent on 17 March; the New Netherland Company builds Fort Nassau on Castle Island near Albany.
pointDescs.1621: The Dutch West India Company is chartered on 3 June with exclusive rights in West Africa and the Americas; Fort Nassau has already been abandoned to floods.
pointDescs.1624: New Netherland becomes a province of the Dutch Republic; 30 families land at Fort Orange and Noten Eylant under the first director, Cornelius Jacobsen May.
pointDescs.1626: Peter Minuit acquires Manhattan on 24 May for goods worth 60 guilders and builds Fort Amsterdam; New Amsterdam grows around it.
pointDescs.1629: The Charter of Freedoms and Exemptions offers patroonships to attract settlers; Rensselaerswyck is the one that succeeds.
pointDescs.1638: Willem Kieft becomes director of a colony that has not flourished; Minuit, dismissed, plants New Sweden on the Delaware for the Swedish crown.
pointDescs.1645: Kieft's War, begun by the massacre of 130 Tappan and Wecquaesgeek at Pavonia and Corlear's Hook, ends in a treaty brokered by the Hackensack sagamore Oratam.
pointDescs.1647: Peter Stuyvesant arrives as director-general; land policy has been liberalised and trade deregulated.
pointDescs.1650: The Treaty of Hartford fixes the eastern border with New England; the population, Native Americans apart, is 4,301.
pointDescs.1653: New Amsterdam receives its municipal charter; the colony grows dramatically through the 1650s as a centre of North Atlantic trade.
pointDescs.1655: Stuyvesant conquers New Sweden and founds New Amstel; Jews gain full residency in New Amsterdam; the Peach War strikes Pavonia and Staten Island.
pointDescs.1664: Richard Nicolls's four frigates take New Amsterdam without resistance on 27 August; on the Delaware Robert Carr sells Dutch prisoners into slavery.
pointDescs.1667: The Treaty of Breda ends the Second Anglo-Dutch War and the Dutch do not press their claim; New Netherland is English, though briefly retaken in 1673–1674.

notes: The register ends the colony in 1667 (Treaty of Breda); the article's own narrative runs to the Dutch recapture of 1673 and the Treaty of Westminster of 1674, which the text and the 1667 point description mention.

The article does not date the Pavonia and Corlear's Hook massacre itself (it falls in Kieft's administration, 1638–1647, and the war ended in 1645 'after two years'), so the massacre is placed under Kieft's War and the 1645 point.

Population figures in the article conflict: 4,301 in 1650 and 8,000–9,000 in 1674 in the lead, but '8,000 population in 1635' and 'about 15,000, including 500 on Manhattan' around 1647 in the body. The lead figures were used.
The article names Minuit's counterparts only as 'unnamed native people, believed to have been Canarsee' (Nathaniel Benchley names Seyseys); the text keeps the article's hedge.
References come from the Further reading list; publishers are given only where the article gives them.
